newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Socialists say bigger EU must reflect social values.
newsitem.headline: Socialists say bigger EU must reflect social values.

text.p: Leaders of European socialist parties meeting in Hungary said on Saturday EU expansion must emphasise social values if the tide of "Euroscepticism" is to be reversed.

"So many people are talking about monetary union...about stabilisation pacts...about Maastricht criteria. This is nothing that the ordinary man on the street understands," Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky told Reuters on the opening day of the two-day conference.
"But there's one very important element that he associates with this, that's the element, of insecurity -- of not knowing what his future will be.

"Therefore I have told my people...it must be the social democrats who carry forward again and again the full employment targets in the union, the social security targets," said Vranitzky, whose country saw the most striking example to date of Euroscepticism with this month's 27.6 percent vote for the anti-Maastricht Freedom Party.

The Party of European Socialists (PES) conference in Budapest brought together prime ministers and party chiefs from 15 EU countries along with Norway, Slovakia, Slovenia, Poland, Czech Republic, Hungary and Cyprus.

"There is a position within the European social democratic parties that we should have a...conclave every year to have a chance...to talk about the long-term perspectives of European integration," PES President Rudolf Scharping, leader of the German opposition Social Democrats, told reporters.
A dozen countries are bidding for membership in an enlarged EU and negotiations should begin at the conclusion of an EU intergovernmental conference which is expected to end in 1997.
Of the east and central European candidates, Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary are usually mentioned as those most likely to negotiate entry terms first.
But Klaus Hansch, president of the European Parliament, told reporters outside the conference's closed-door sessions that aspiring EU members should not expect any favoritism.
"There is no compromising," Hansch said. "These countries will have to join the EU as it is."
Hansch said Hungary should be aware it may run into difficulties in its negotiations because of the extensive Hungarian farm subsidy programme.
And he said Slovakia was taking the wrong approach if it thought it could negotiate entry and then make democratic reforms sought by the EU.
"Slovakia wants to join the EU and then make reforms, but we want them to make the reforms first and join afterwards," Hansch told Reuters.

Earlier this week Slovakia's ruling coalition approved two laws criticised by the EU and the United States, one boosting powers of the public prosecutor and the other giving the Education Ministry broad control over academic affairs.
Vranitzky attributed the Freedom Party's showing in Austria in part to lack of a protest vote, since his Social Democrats share power with the conservative People's Party.
Other socialists said discontent is widespread.
"The present EU is not offering the people enough, that's obvious when you look at election results," said Jan Marinus Wiersma, a PES official.
"We must take this into account not by pulling the brake, but by saying we have to move forward in certain areas, especially in those areas where people expect something," he said.
